steps.caption: White to move, move ten of a French Exchange. Look at the pawns, not the pieces. One file has no pawns of either colour. Find it before you read on.

claims.statement: The e-file is the only open file; every other file still holds a pawn of at least one side.
The engine rates the position as about equal (depth 16).

steps.prompt: Before any explanation: which file would you like a rook on, and which square on it could the rook land on? Do not worry about being right. You will come back to this at the end.

fields.label: A square my rook could land on, and why it might fail:

steps.text: **Today's question.** An open file is a road with no pawns on it. Roads lead somewhere, or nowhere. By the end you will look at a position and say which file is worth a rook, which square the rook will land on, who can stop it, and what each side does about it. First, learn to see the road at all.

steps.caption: White to move. No pawn of either colour stands on the e-file, so it is open. Every other file still has pawns, so those files are closed. Either rook can use the open file.

line.say: The rook on a1 steps onto the open file. Nothing can block it on the way up.

claims.statement: The e-file is open and no other file is open or half-open.
Exactly two moves put a rook on the open file: the rook on a1 or the rook on f1 goes to e1.

steps.caption: Same pawns, one rook already on e1. Count the squares each rook can move to. The rook on the open file has room; the rook on a1 has its own pawn in front of it and its own rook at the end of the rank.

claims.statement: The rook on e1 can move to 11 squares.
The rook on a1 can move to only 3 squares.

steps.caption: Rooks on e1 and f1. The lit squares are the open file the rook on e1 attacks. It sees all the way to e8: the file is a road into Black's camp.

line.say: The rook slides the whole file and lands on e7. No black piece attacks that square.
Black moves the pawn the rook was attacking.
The second rook joins the first on the same file, behind it.

claims.statement: The rook on e1 attacks every square of the e-file up to e8.
No black piece attacks e7.
From e7 the rook attacks the pawn on b7.

steps.caption: A position from a 2021 broadcast game (we could not re-find the game, so treat it as an illustration). White to move. Read the files: which is open, which is half-open for White (no white pawn, but a black one), which for Black?

claims.statement: The c-file is open, the b-file is half-open for White and the d-file is half-open for Black.

steps.text: **A road, not a prize.** A rook on an open file with no way in still ties pieces down; it just does not win material by itself. What matters is where it can *land* in the enemy camp: its **entry square**. A common best landing [I] is the seventh rank, where the enemy pawns start and the king is boxed in. Aron Nimzowitsch's *My System* treats a file as a way to reach a point [S]. Ask: which square, and who watches it?

steps.title: Same rook, one change
steps.prompt: Black's knight stands on e8 instead of h5. Does Rc7 still win a pawn? Predict first, then check.

steps.caption: White to move. The d-file is open and no black piece attacks d7. Black's knight on e4 is also loose, so White is better for two reasons; the entry is one of them [I]. Follow the rook.

line.say: The rook lands on d7, an entry square no black piece watches. It attacks the pawns on b7 and f7.
Black pushes one attacked pawn forward. The pawn on a7 was never defended: the pawn on b7 only blocked the rook's view along the rank. Now the rook sees it.
The rook takes the pawn on a7. The landing paid off.

claims.statement: No black piece attacks d7.
From d7 the rook attacks the pawn on b7.
From d7 the rook attacks the pawn on f7.
After the pawn push, the pawn on a7 is attacked and undefended.
Landing on d7 wins at least a pawn along the engine line.
Landing on d7 is among the engine's first choices (depth 16).

steps.text: **When it usually works.** Three things usually need to hold [I]. Your rook reaches the file before the enemy contests it. The entry square is not guarded by a pawn or a minor piece. And something is waiting there: loose pawns, or a king with no room to move. If one is missing, ask what else makes up for it; a landing with tempo or a forcing follow-up can still work.

steps.caption: Compare with the board before: the same idea with a bishop on e5 instead of the knight on e4. The bishop does not attack d7. White to move.

line.say: The rook lands on d7. The bishop on e5 does not attack that square.
The rook switches along the file to attack the bishop and the pawn on b5 together.

claims.statement: No black piece attacks d7.
Landing on d7 wins at least a pawn along the engine line.
From d5 the rook attacks the bishop on e5.
From d5 the rook also attacks the pawn on b5.
Landing on d7 is the engine's first choice (depth 16).
The engine prefers White by between a half and two and a half pawns (depth 16).

steps.caption: The d-file is open. Black's pawns on c7 and e7 guard the square d6, so a rook could not safely stop there. Does that stop it from landing on d7? White to move.

line.say: The rook jumps over the guarded square d6 and lands on d7. A rook moves through attacked squares as long as they are empty.
Black adds a defender to the pawn on c7.
The second rook joins the first. The pawn on e7 is still under attack.

claims.statement: Two black pawns guard d6.
No black piece attacks d7.
The rook on d7 attacks the pawn on e7.
The rook move to d7 is the engine's first choice (depth 16).

line.say: The second rook lands on c7 and attacks the bishop on d7. Nothing black attacks that square.
The bishop moves away from the attack.

claims.statement: No black piece attacks c7.
From c7 the rook attacks the bishop on d7.
Doubling on the seventh rank is the engine's first choice (depth 16).

steps.text: **Why the seventh rank? [I]** Three reasons, in our reading. No enemy pawn can guard a square there, because pawns never stand on their own back rank; only pieces can. The pawns still at home can be attacked from the side. And the king is often boxed in behind them, so two rooks there can threaten mate. Edward Lasker, in *Chess Strategy*, says the side whose rooks reach the file first gets the raids on the seventh [S].

**When the landing is a trap [I].** A rook on the seventh can be cut off. If a bishop or knight attacks it, its retreat squares are covered, and the king or a pawn guards the squares beside it, the rook may be lost for a piece. Before you land, ask not only who attacks the square now but where the rook goes if it is attacked next. [H] This may cost club players more rooks than a slow arrival does. (No board yet: unchecked idea.)

**Remember.** An open file has no pawns of either colour on it. It is a road, not a prize, so ask where your rook can land: the entry square, often on the seventh rank. Check that no pawn or minor piece guards it and that something is waiting there. Also ask where the rook goes if it is attacked.
